Empirical Research Plan  
“Carbon Pricing and Economic Outcomes: Distributional Impacts across Regions, Sectors, and Consumers”  

----------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with exposure-weighted treatment intensity, complemented by an event-study specification for dynamics.

Why DiD?
• The policy arrives at an identifiable moment (or staggered moments) but its bite differs systematically across regions/sectors because of pre-existing carbon-emission intensity.  
• This cross-sectional heterogeneity, interacted with the before/after time dimension, delivers the classic DiD counterfactual (“low-exposure units show how high-exposure units would have evolved absent the policy”).  
• The data contain multiple pre-policy periods, allowing us to test the parallel-trend assumption and to trace the treatment effect over time (event study).  

Optional robustness:  
• Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) at the statutory emissions threshold (e.g., installations emitting ≥ X tCO₂ fall under the price) to obtain a local treatment effect.  
• Instrumental-variables Bartik approach (carbon price × baseline intensity) to address endogeneity of realized cost pass-through.

----------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TREAT_rs = POST_t × EXPOSURE_rs  
where  
• POST_t = 1 for years ≥ first year of carbon pricing in region r; 0 otherwise.  
• EXPOSURE_rs = baseline emission intensity of sector s in region r (tCO₂ per unit output, measured 2–3 years pre-policy).

Interpretation: a one-unit increase in exposure raises the marginal cost of carbon by CarbonPrice × Exposure; β captures the semi-elasticity of outcome Y wrt that cost.

Control group  
Units with relatively low EXPOSURE_rs (lowest tercile, or continuous scaling in the regression) act as the counterfactual. They face the same macro shocks and nationwide policies but very small carbon-cost pressure.

Treatment timing  
• If the carbon price started nationwide on 1 Jan 2016, POST_t = 1 from 2016 onward.  
• If different regions entered at different dates, POST_t becomes region-specific and we use a staggered-adoption DiD with unit × year fixed effects.

RDD variant (robustness)  
Running variable: pre-policy annual emissions at the installation or firm level.  
Cut-off: statutory threshold E* (e.g., 25,000 tCO₂).  
Treatment: CarbonPrice applies iff Emissions ≥ E*.

----------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the policy, high- and low-exposure sectors/regions would follow parallel outcome paths.  
• Plausibility: Baseline exposure measured before any knowledge of the policy; multiple pre-policy years available for testing.

A2. Exogeneity of baseline exposure: Pre-policy intensity is not chosen in anticipation of the carbon price.  
• Plausibility: Policy announcement occurred after the baseline window; historical intensity largely reflects technological vintage and resource mix.

A3. No differential contemporaneous shocks correlated with exposure.  
• Plausibility: Must verify that other policies (renewable subsidies, recession shocks) are not systematically targeted to carbon-intensive sectors.

A4. Stable composition (no large entry/exit biasing the sample).  
• Plausibility: Use balanced panel or inverse probability weights; check attrition patterns.

A5. SUTVA / limited spillovers: Outcomes in low-exposure units are not affected by high-exposure units’ carbon costs (e.g., via input–output linkages).  
• Plausibility: Some upstream pass-through is possible; we can incorporate supply-chain controls or cluster standard errors at a higher level.

----------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------
T1. Pre-trends or mean-reversion correlated with exposure.  
• Mitigation: Graphical and regression-based pre-trend tests; include sector-specific linear time trends; placebo policy dates.

T2. Anticipation/stockpiling before implementation.  
• Mitigation: Drop the year immediately preceding implementation or include a lead dummy; test for significant leads in the event study.

T3. Concurrent policies (renewable portfolio standards, industry bail-outs).  
• Mitigation: Collect policy dummies and interact with exposure; double-robust specifications; difference-in-differences-in-differences (DDD) using unaffected sectors in neighboring countries as an additional control.

----------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # fast fixed-effects DiD
library(ggplot2)
library(did)          # Callaway & Sant’Anna, if staggered adoption
# Optional: library(rdrobust)

# 1. Data -------------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("carbon_policy_panel.csv")   # assume region-sector-year data

# 2. Variable Construction --------------------------------------------------
# Policy start year (could be region-specific)
policy_year <- 2016                  
dt[, post := as.integer(year >= policy_year)]

# Baseline exposure: average emissions intensity, 3 yrs pre-policy
dt[, exposure := mean(emissions_intensity[year %in% (policy_year-3):(policy_year-1)]),
   by = .(region, sector)]

# Interaction term
dt[, treat_intensity := post * exposure]

# Normalize outcomes (logs where appropriate)
dt[, ln_output := log(sector_output)]
dt[, ln_employment := log(employment)]
dt[, ln_price := log(consumer_price_index)]

# 3. Main DiD Regression ----------------------------------------------------
# Sector-region & year fixed effects; clustered SEs (region*sector)
did_out <- feols(ln_output ~ treat_intensity | region^sector + year,
                 data = dt, cluster = ~region_sector)

summary(did_out)

# 4. Event-Study (Dynamics) -------------------------------------------------
# Create relative year
dt[, rel_year := year - policy_year]

# Build event-time dummies (leave out -1 as reference)
for(k in -5:5) if(k != -1) dt[, paste0("rel_",k) := as.integer(rel_year == k)]

# Interaction with exposure (Sun & Abraham style)
event_formula <- as.formula(
  paste("ln_output ~ ",
        paste(paste0("rel_", setdiff(-5:5, -1), ":exposure"), collapse = " + "),
        "| region^sector + year"))

event_out <- feols(event_formula, data = dt, cluster = ~region_sector)

iplot(event_out)  # visualization of dynamic β_k

# 5. Robustness: RDD around statutory cutoff -------------------------------
# Sub-sample within ±20% of threshold (Estar)
Estar <- 25000
dt_rdd <- dt[abs(prepolicy_emissions - Estar) <= 0.2*Estar & year == policy_year]

# rdrobust (if installation-level data available)
# rd_out <- rdrobust(y = dt_rdd$ln_output,
#                    x = dt_rdd$prepolicy_emissions - Estar)

# 6. Robustness: Alternative exposure measure ------------------------------
dt[, exposure_z := scale(exposure)]   # z-score standardization
did_alt <- feols(ln_output ~ post*exposure_z | region^sector + year,
                 data = dt, cluster = ~region_sector)
etable(did_out, did_alt, tex = FALSE)
```

----------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts:  
• High-exposure (carbon-intensive) sectors face cost increases → output and employment decline relative to low-exposure sectors; consumer prices for energy-intensive goods rise.  
• Magnitude: A €10/tCO₂ increase (~5 ¢ per kWh of coal electricity) could reduce sectoral gross output by 1-3 % in the short run (elasticities −0.1 to −0.3). Employment effects likely smaller (labour hoarding), perhaps −0.5 %. Consumer price pass-through roughly 50 % of the marginal cost shock.

----------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
(C1–C5 adapted from authoritative DiD guidelines)

C1: Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically supported……….. 1  
C2: No anticipation / policy announced close to implementation….. 0.5  
C3: No time-varying confounders correlated with exposure……….. 0.5  
C4: Stable units & no spillovers across treatment statuses……….. 0.5  
C5: Correct timing and coding of treatment……………………………. 1  
Total (out of 5)……………………………………………………………. 3.5  

Interpretation: Assumptions look plausible but threats (C2–C4) require careful robustness work described above.
